title: Infantile Scabies in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Observations From the First Case Report
case_text:
A 4-month-old boy was referred by his mother in December 2023 to Ngamanzo Hospital, in the northern suburb of Kinshasa (capital of DRC), due to a cutaneous eruption. He was the only infant in the family who lived with his parents in the village of Ngamanzo, approximately 55 km from the capital, where according to local health authorities, there were many cases of scabies infestation. The family used to sleep altogether on a sponge mattress placed on the floor. Moreover, the infant was showering twice a day and wearing socks. Additionally, there was a notion of itching and bedbug infestation at home. The infant was afebrile with a good general condition.
Initial clinical examination of the infant and interrogation of the parents revealed irritability, insomnia, pustule-like skin rashes on the soles of the feet and palms of the hands, associated with multiple scaly lesions on the wrist and interdigital spaces that had been exhibited for a month (Figure 1A,B).
His mother was clinically examined as well, presenting erythemato-papular eruptions all over the body and scaly lesions on the wrists and interdigital spaces with recurrent nocturnal pruritus. Conversely, his father showed no clinical signs of scabies infestation.
Parasitological examination using a dermatoscope revealed the scabies burrows on the palm of the right hand. The female S. scabiei mites and eggs were isolated from the infant and his mother after microscopic examination under 100x magnification of scale scraping (Figure 1C,D).
Symptoms such as irritability and insomnia, along with severe pruritic and polymorphic skin lesions, allow for differentiating infantile scabies.
Treatment with the topical application of ascabiol (benzyl benzoate 10%) on Day (D) 0 and D8 for the infant and with ivermectin (200 mug/kg) on D0 and D10 for the parents prevented recurrence of infestation and resulted in a favorable outcome 2 weeks later.

   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Scabies
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: infantile scabies
